  collapse = TRUE,

```

Many variables observed once a year depend on drought. Tree-ring widths,
crop yields, the annual flow of a river or the level of a reservoir at the
end of the summer are examples. Each of them responds to the water balance
of a particular part of the year, accumulated over a particular length of
time. A crop may depend on the rain of the three months before harvest. A
reservoir may integrate the water balance of a whole year.

The SPEI and the SPI can be computed at many time scales. The value of the
index in a given month at a time scale of `s` months summarizes the water
balance of the `s` months ending in that month. So the index at a month
and a time scale defines a window of time. Correlating the annual series
with the index in every month and at every time scale shows which window
the series responds to most. The function `scale_scan()` does this, and
`scale_extract()` gives the index series of the chosen window.

This approach has been used to relate the SPEI and the SPI to tree-ring
growth across a climatic gradient (Pasho et al., 2011), to map the time
scales at which vegetation responds to drought across the world's biomes
(Vicente-Serrano et al., 2013), and to study how thinning changes the
sensitivity of tree growth to hydric and thermal stress in four widely
planted pine species (Manrique-Alba et al., 2025).

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(SPEI)

data(wichita)
wichita <- ts(wichita[, -c(1, 2)], start = c(1980, 1), frequency = 12)
bal <- wichita[, "PRCP"] - hargreaves(wichita[, "TMIN"], wichita[, "TMAX"],
  lat = 37.6475, verbose = FALSE
)
```

The package has no annual series to correlate with the `wichita` climate.
All the annual series in this vignette are **synthetic**. They are built
from the water balance of Wichita plus random noise, so that we know which
window they respond to. A small helper adds up the water balance of some
months for each year, and standardizes it:

```{r}
years <- 1980:2011

# Standardized sum of `x` over `months`, for each year in `years`;
# `back = 1` takes the months of the previous year.
season <- function(x, months, back = 0) {
  sel <- cycle(x) %in% months
  v <- tapply(x[sel], floor(time(x))[sel], sum)
  v <- v[as.character(years - back)]
  as.numeric((v - mean(v, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(v, na.rm = TRUE))
}
```

## The annual series

The annual series must contain only the signal that we want to relate to
drought. Other sources of variation over time should be removed first.
Crop yields usually grow over the years because of better varieties and
management. Tree rings get narrower as the tree grows older. These trends
are not related to drought, but they add variance to the series, and they
can create spurious correlations with any index that also has a trend.

Our first synthetic series is a crop yield. It grows by 0.05 t/ha per year,
and it responds to the water balance of May to July (three months ending
in July):

```{r}
set.seed(2)
yield <- 3 + 0.05 * (years - 1980) + 0.4 * season(bal, 5:7) +
  rnorm(length(years), sd = 0.3)
yield <- ts(yield, start = 1980, frequency = 1)
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Synthetic crop yield from 1980 to 2011, with an increasing trend"}
plot(yield, ylab = "Yield (t/ha)", xlab = "Year")
```

The annual series is a time series with frequency 1, or a data frame with
the years in the first column and the values in the second.

## Running the scan

`scale_scan()` takes the water balance, computes the SPEI at the time
scales in `scales`, and correlates the annual series with the index in each
month and at each time scale:

```{r}
sc <- scale_scan(bal, yield, scales = 1:24)
sc
```

No window is significant. The trend in the yield hides the climate signal.
With `detrend = TRUE` a linear trend is removed from the annual series
before computing the correlations:

```{r}
sc <- scale_scan(bal, yield, scales = 1:24, detrend = TRUE)
sc
```

The linear detrending is enough here, because the synthetic trend is
linear. Real series often need other methods, such as splines for
tree-ring widths. In that case detrend the series before calling
`scale_scan()`, and leave `detrend = FALSE`.

## Reading the heatmap

The `plot` method draws the correlations as a heatmap. The months are on
the horizontal axis and the time scales on the vertical axis. The dots
mark the cells that are significant after adjusting for multiple testing,
and the black outlines show the best windows:

```{r, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the correlation between the detrended yield and the SPEI by month and time scale. The highest correlations are in July at short time scales."}
plot(sc)
```

The strongest correlations are around July at short time scales, as
expected. They fade at longer time scales, which add months that do not
affect the yield. With `sig = "mask"` the non-significant cells are left
blank.

The results are kept in the object. `sc$cor` holds the correlations, with
one row per month and one column per time scale. `sc$p` and `sc$p.adj`
hold the p-values before and after the adjustment, and `sc$n` the number
of years used in each cell.

```{r}
round(sc$cor[5:9, 1:6], 2)
```

## The best windows and multiple testing

The best windows are the cells with the highest and the lowest
correlation, among those that are significant:

```{r}
sc$best
```

The scan above tests `r sum(!is.na(sc$cor))` cells. With so many tests,
some cells will have a low p-value by chance. At a 5% level, about 14 of
288 cells would be 'significant' with an annual series of pure noise. For
this reason the p-values are adjusted for multiple testing, across all the
cells. The default method, Holm's, keeps the probability of any false
positive among all the cells below `alpha`. Other methods can be chosen
with `p.adjust` (see `?p.adjust`). With `p.adjust = "none"` many more cells
are marked, but most of them are only neighbours of the best one:

```{r}
sc_none <- scale_scan(bal, yield, scales = 1:24, detrend = TRUE,
  p.adjust = "none"
)
sum(sc_none$p.adj <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(sc$p.adj <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The adjustment is conservative, because neighbouring cells share most of
their data. With short series it may leave no significant cell even when
there is a real signal. The unadjusted p-values are always in `sc$p`.

## Conditions of the previous year

Some annual series also depend on the conditions of the previous year. Tree
growth, for example, often depends on the water stored at the end of the
previous growing season. Time scales longer than the month reach into the
previous year (a time scale of 12 in March covers April of the previous
year to March), but they always include the months of the current year
too. The argument `lag` scans the months of previous years directly:
`lag = 0:1` correlates the annual series of year Y with the index of year
Y and of year Y-1.

Our second synthetic series is a tree-ring index that responds to the water
balance of July to September of the previous year:

```{r}
set.seed(5)
rings <- 1 + 0.2 * season(bal, 7:9, back = 1) +
  rnorm(length(years), sd = 0.1)
rings <- ts(rings, start = 1980, frequency = 1)
```

```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the correlation between the synthetic tree-ring index and the SPEI, for the months of the previous and the current year. The highest correlation is in September of the previous year."}
sc_lag <- scale_scan(bal, rings, scales = 1:12, lag = 0:1)
sc_lag$best
plot(sc_lag)
```

The rows are now in chronological order. `Jan-1` to `Dec-1` are the
months of the previous year, and `Jan` to `Dec` those of the current year.
The best window is found in September of the previous year at a time scale
of three months. The `lag` column of `best` gives the year. The adjustment
of the p-values covers all the cells, so the scan with `lag = 0:1` is
stricter than one with `lag = 0`.

## Extracting the series of a window

`scale_extract()` returns the annual series of the index for a window, by
default the best positive one. It is aligned with the annual series: for a
window with a lag of one year, the value of year Y is the index of year
Y-1.

```{r}
spei_best <- scale_extract(sc_lag)
spei_best
```

The series covers all the years of the climate data, shifted by the lag
(here 1981 to 2012), so it does not span the same years as the annual
series. Use `ts.intersect()` to align them by year before using them
together in other models. Note that `lm()` does not align time series by
itself.

```{r}
d <- ts.intersect(rings, spei_best)
fit <- lm(rings ~ spei_best, data = d)
summary(fit)$r.squared
```

Plotting the two series together shows how closely the index of the best
window follows the annual series. They are in different units, so here the
ring series is standardized (mean 0, standard deviation 1) to plot it on
the scale of the index:

```{r, fig.alt = "Time plot of the standardized synthetic ring-width series and the SPEI of the best window (previous September, 3-month scale), which follow each other closely"}
rings_std <- (rings - mean(rings, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(rings, na.rm = TRUE)
plot(spei_best, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2,
  ylim = range(c(spei_best, rings_std), na.rm = TRUE),
  xlab = "Year", ylab = "Standardized value"
)
lines(rings_std, col = "black", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
legend("bottomleft", c("Ring width (standardized)", "SPEI, best window"),
  col = c("black", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n"
)
```

Any other window can be extracted by giving `cycle`, `scale` and `lag`:

```{r}
spei_jul6 <- scale_extract(sc_lag, cycle = 7, scale = 6, lag = 0)
```

The correlation of the best window is chosen as the highest of many. It is
biased upwards, so the strength of the relationship should be checked with
independent data when possible.

## Options of the index

Options for `spei()` can be passed through `scale_scan()`, for example a
reference period or a kernel. With `index = "spi"` the SPI is computed
instead, from a precipitation series.

```{r}
sc_spi <- scale_scan(wichita[, "PRCP"], yield,
  scales = 1:12, index = "spi",
  detrend = TRUE, distribution = "PearsonIII"
)
sc_spi$best
```

The index can also be computed beforehand and passed with
`index = "precomputed"`, as a time series with one column per time scale.
The time scales are taken from the column names, or given in `scales`:

```{r}
idx <- sapply(c(1, 3, 6, 12), function(s) {
  spei(bal, s, verbose = FALSE)$fitted
})
idx <- ts(idx, start = c(1980, 1), frequency = 12)
colnames(idx) <- c("SPEI-1", "SPEI-3", "SPEI-6", "SPEI-12")
scale_scan(idx, yield, index = "precomputed", detrend = TRUE)$best
```

This is useful to scan an index computed elsewhere, or a set of time scales
computed once and used for several annual series.

## Other frequencies

The scan is not limited to monthly data. The position of each value in the
year comes from the frequency of the time series. Weekly data (frequency
52) give one row per week, labelled `W1` to `W52`, and `W1-1` to `W52-1`
for the previous year. The time scales are then in weeks:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# bal_week: a weekly water balance, as a ts with frequency 52
sc_week <- scale_scan(bal_week, rings, scales = seq(2, 52, by = 2))
```

## Several annual series

Often there are several series for the same site, such as several trees, or
several fields of the same crop. There are two ways to analyse them.

The first one is to average them into a single series, and scan it once.
`y` can be a time series with one column per series, a data frame with the
years in the first column and one column per series, or a data frame with
repeated years (one row per year and series). All the values of each year
are averaged. `y.count` keeps the number of values in each year.

Our synthetic 'trees' share a common signal, the water balance of April
to June, and each one has its own noise. The noise is large, as it is in
real trees:

```{r}
set.seed(11)
common <- season(bal, 4:6)
trees <- sapply(1:8, function(i) 0.5 * common + rnorm(length(years)))
colnames(trees) <- paste0("tree", 1:8)
trees <- ts(trees, start = 1980, frequency = 1)

sc_mean <- scale_scan(bal, trees, scales = 1:12)
sc_mean$best
```

The second one is to scan each series on its own:

```{r}
per_tree <- lapply(colnames(trees), function(tr) {
  scale_scan(bal, trees[, tr], scales = 1:12)$best[1, ]
})
per_tree <- do.call(rbind, per_tree)
cbind(tree = colnames(trees), per_tree[, c("label", "scale", "r", "p.adj")])
```

The average has a much stronger and more stable signal than any single
tree, because the individual noise cancels out. This is the standard way
of building tree-ring chronologies. But averaging is only valid if all the
series share the same climate data and respond to it in a similar way. It
also hides any difference between sites or individuals. If the series are
on different scales, standardize them before averaging.

Scanning each series gives a window for each one, so it can reveal
different responses, and each series can have its own climate data. But
each scan has more noise, and there are more tests in total. In the
example above, the windows of the single trees are scattered, and some
trees have no significant window, although all of them respond to the same
months.
